bibliography.abstract: Motor insurance is a legal requirement in order to operate vehicles on public roads in most developed countries. Thus, motor insurers play an important, yet understudied, role in transport governance, including the governance of innovations around connected, automated, shared and electric mobility. This paper offers an empirical enquiry into the role of motor insurers in future (personal) transport developments. Utilising 40 semi-structured interviews with insurers and stakeholders in the United Kingdom we address two questions: 1) how do insurers and near stakeholders view the future of mobility; and 2) what role do they see for themselves in this future, and can they enact that role in a shifting insurance landscape. Interviewees describe a mobility sphere in flux, with a wide variety of innovations that concern them and in which they see a key role for themselves across three domains: legal (insurance as obligation), safety (insurance policies and data practices as a way to monitor and guide towards safer mobility) and risk management (financial compensation). Approaches to managing the changing landscape differ; whilst some insurers discuss, and provide insurance products for, new innovations well in advance of them becoming mainstay, others have them lower down their priority list. This appetite to address and facilitate future mobility affects the ease with which some developments in the mobility sphere progress and (in)directly influences the future of our mobility. As such, they act as gatekeepers of some, if not most, future mobility developments.
bibliography.title: Motor insurers: gatekeepers of future mobility?

en.caveats: The findings are based on qualitative interview data from a single national context, which may reflect the specific regulatory and market conditions of the United Kingdom.
en.what: This study investigates the role of motor insurers in shaping transport governance and future mobility innovations through 40 semi-structured interviews with insurers and stakeholders in the United Kingdom. It maps how these actors view emerging connected, automated, shared, and electric mobility trends, identifying three key domains of influence: legal obligations, safety monitoring via data practices, and financial risk management.
en.why: It demonstrates that insurers act as active gatekeepers whose varying appetite for risk and product innovation directly accelerates or hinders the adoption of new transport technologies.
